song.title: Paint It Black
song.album: Aftermath (US release; not on the original UK LP, released internationally as a standalone single)

guitar.guitaristsText: Keith Richards (electric & acoustic guitars) / Brian Jones (sitar — the track's signature lead instrument; acoustic guitar contribution is contested between sources)
guitar.type: Solid-body/semi-solid electric (Richards) plus acoustic guitar; the track's actual lead hook is a genuine Indian sitar (Jones), not a guitar effect
guitar.modelsText: Gibson Les Paul Custom 'Black Beauty' (3-pickup) or Gibson Firebird VII — both documented as Richards' main guitars in the Aftermath/Between the Buttons era (Richards); genuine sitar, exact instrument/model unconfirmed (Jones)
guitar.evidence: Wikipedia's personnel section for 'Paint It Black' (citing Andy Babiuk & Greg Prevost, 'Rolling Stones Gear', 2013) credits Richards with electric and acoustic guitars and Jones with sitar and acoustic guitar; a second source (Margotin & Guesdon, 'The Rolling Stones All the Songs', 2016) confirms the sitar credit but places a question mark on Jones' guitar contribution specifically. Era gear profiles (Ground Guitar, Guitar Lobby, Guitar World) document Richards using three-pickup Gibson Les Paul Customs and a reverse-body Firebird VII during the Aftermath/Between the Buttons period, having phased out his Epiphone Casino by late 1965.
guitar.notes: Major corrections to the original sheet: (1) Ronnie Wood and Mick Taylor did NOT play on this track — Wood joined the Stones in 1975 and Taylor in 1969, both years after this March 1966 recording; they were removed entirely. (2) The Telecaster 'Micawber' and 5-string open-G tuning are anachronistic for this session — that rig belongs to Richards' post-1968/early-1970s era (e.g., 'Street Fighting Man' onward), not 1966. (3) Most importantly, the song's iconic hook is a real sitar played by Brian Jones, not a guitar processed to sound sitar-like — this reframes the entire tone/rig approach below.
guitar.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint_It_Black (personnel, citing Babiuk & Prevost 2013 and Margotin & Guesdon 2016); groundguitar.com and guitarlobby.com Keith Richards gear histories; guitarworld.com 'Keith Richards: A Life in Guitars'

tone.target: hypnotic, driving raga-rock groove: a real sitar drone (Brian Jones) over clean-to-edge-of-breakup rhythm guitar, throbbing bass/Hammond pedal tones and hand percussion — not a guitar-riff song in the conventional sense
tone.profile: clean-to-edge-of-breakup Vox-style rhythm guitar supporting (not replacing) a genuine sitar lead
tone.summary: The GP-180 patch below targets the one element that is genuinely reproducible on a guitar multi-fx unit: Keith Richards' documented rhythm/electric guitar part, played through a period-correct Vox AC30 Top Boost with light overdrive and a driving eighth-note strum. The sitar hook itself — the song's actual signature sound — cannot be authentically recreated by a guitar amp/cab/EQ chain and is flagged separately under improvements.
mustHave: driving eighth-note strummed rhythm, clear and defined
light, low-level overdrive only — not heavy drive
tight low end so the part doesn't compete with the bass/Hammond pedal
avoid: heavy fuzz or high-gain distortion (not documented for this track — that's 'Satisfaction', a different song/pedal)
thick chorus or heavy modulation on the core rhythm patch
presenting a processed guitar as a literal substitute for the real sitar
gearClues: Vox AC30 Top Boost — the period- and endorsement-appropriate amp most consistently cited for mid-60s Stones sessions; GP-180 has a direct 'AC30 TB' model
light overdrive only; no fuzz pedal is documented for this specific song
capo on the 2nd fret with Dm-shaped chords (sounding in E minor) is the standard practical teaching approach, though not confirmed as the exact 1966 studio method
a real sitar (Brian Jones) carries the actual lead hook — outside the scope of any guitar-only rig
corrections: Dropped the original 'sitar-like guitar' framing as the primary goal — the recording uses an actual sitar, which no guitar amp modeler can genuinely reproduce; reframed the patch around Richards' documented rhythm guitar part instead.

Replaced 'blues rock' as the song's identity with its actual classification (psychedelic rock / raga rock per the Wikipedia infobox); multiple contemporary reviews and later scholarship describe this track as an explicit break from the Stones' usual blues-rock/garage-rock formula.
Removed the generic 'British crunch' / heavy distortion assumption — no reliable source documents fuzz or heavy drive on this track specifically.
Replaced the vague 'small amp' clue with the specific, sourced Vox AC30 Top Boost, which also happens to exist as a named model in the GP-180 catalog (AC30 TB).

rig.name: The Rolling Stones - Paint It Black - Valeton GP-180
rig.recommendedGuitar: Solid-body/semi-hollow Gibson-style guitar (Les Paul Custom or Firebird-style) for the rhythm part. Important: the song's signature hook is a real sitar (Brian Jones) and cannot be authentically reproduced on a standard 6-string — for the lead hook, use a dedicated electric sitar (e.g., Coral/Danelectro Electric Sitar), a sitar VST/sample library, or a sitar-emulation pedal layered separately from this guitar patch.

blocks.purpose: Light noise gate; the tone is clean-to-edge-of-breakup, so minimal gating is needed.
Adds the 'slight overdrive' texture guitar-lesson sources describe for Richards' tone here, kept low so the chords stay clear and defined rather than driven.
blocks.gap: No specific pedal is documented for this track; this is a low-gain vintage-voiced approximation of the light edge described by secondary sources.

alternatives.reason: A light compressor could substitute if you want more sustain/evenness than added grit.

blocks.purpose: Included to fill the required WAH slot; no evidence ties a wah pedal to this track.
blocks.gap: No source documents wah use on this recording.

blocks.purpose: Included to fill the required DST slot but left inactive.
blocks.gap: A fan tone-database entry claims a Maestro FZ-1-style fuzz 'main riff' on this song, but that pedal/description is the well-documented signature of 'Satisfaction' (1965), a different track — likely a source confusion. No reliable interview or session document ties fuzz to 'Paint It Black' specifically, so it is kept inactive here.

alternatives.reason: Only engage if you specifically want the (unconfirmed) fuzz-guitar interpretation some fan sources describe.

blocks.purpose: Vox AC30 Top Boost is the amp most consistently cited for mid-60s Stones recordings (the band had a Vox endorsement deal through this era); GP-180's AC30 TB model is a direct name match.
blocks.gap: The Stones' own Vox endorsement is well documented for their UK/European live rig of this period; it is not confirmed by a primary source that this exact amp was in the room at RCA Studios Hollywood for the March 1966 sessions specifically — treat as period-plausible rather than session-confirmed.

alternatives.reason: Alternate GP-180 Vox-flavored voicing if AC30 TB feels too polished/modern.

blocks.purpose: Matches the 2x12 combo speaker configuration of a real Vox AC30, keeping the cabinet paired sensibly with the AC30 TB amp block.
blocks.gap: No cabinet model in this catalog is explicitly labeled 'Vox'; Foxy 2x12 is chosen for matching the correct speaker count/format rather than a confirmed IR capture of the actual session cab.

alternatives.reason: Best option if loaded with a real captured Vox AC30 2x12 IR for closer accuracy.

blocks.purpose: Trims low end so the rhythm guitar sits alongside Wyman's heavy bass/Hammond pedal tones without competing, while keeping upper-mid clarity for the strummed chords.
blocks.gap: No specific EQ curve is documented for this session; values are a reasonable estimate based on the song's overall mix balance, not measured from the master.

blocks.purpose: Included to fill the required MOD slot; left inactive on the core, historically-grounded rhythm-guitar patch.
blocks.gap: No modulation is documented on the actual guitar recording. Some users may want to engage a light Tremolo or O-Phase purely as an artistic 'sitar-esque wavering' trick — this is a creative workaround, not a historical reproduction, and should be understood as such.

alternatives.reason: Alternative artistic sitar-adjacent texture; equally undocumented for the real recording.

blocks.purpose: Included to fill the required DLY slot; kept off — no delay is documented for this track.
blocks.gap: No source ties any delay effect to this recording.

blocks.purpose: A light spring reverb is more period-accurate than a generic room verb for a 1966 Vox-era guitar tone (Vox amps of this era commonly had built-in spring tanks); kept subtle to preserve the dry, driving character of the mix.
blocks.gap: Not confirmed for this specific session, but spring reverb is a much better era fit than a modern room/plate algorithm.

alternatives.reason: Use if Spring sounds too 'boingy'; RCA Hollywood's natural room sound is also plausible.

improvements.summary: The single biggest gap is structural, not tonal: this GP-180 patch reproduces Richards' rhythm guitar, but the song's actual signature sound — Brian Jones' sitar — is an entirely different instrument that no guitar rig can genuinely replicate. Secondary priorities refine the Vox-amp approximation.

proposals.recommendedAsset: Coral/Danelectro Electric Sitar, a sitar VST/sample library, or a dedicated sitar-emulation pedal, layered separately from the GP-180 guitar patch
proposals.reason: The GP-180 has no sitar model and cannot reproduce a real sitar's sympathetic strings and buzzing bridge (jawari); this is the single most identifiable element of the recording and is entirely outside the scope of a guitar amp/cab/EQ chain.
proposals.whenToUse: Before treating this GP-180 patch as a full reproduction of the recorded song — it covers the rhythm guitar layer only.
proposals.expectedGain: The only way to genuinely capture the song's defining hook; without it, the patch is a rhythm-guitar tone, not 'the Paint It Black sound'.

proposals.recommendedAsset: User IR 1 loaded with a captured real Vox AC30 2x12 IR
proposals.reason: Foxy 2x12 is a naming/speaker-count approximation rather than a confirmed Vox capture; a dedicated Vox IR would tighten up the chime and top-end character.
proposals.whenToUse: After confirming the AC30 TB amp block feels right for the rhythm part.
proposals.expectedGain: More accurate high-end chime and cabinet resonance.

proposals.target: Exact 1966 guitar model and session amp
proposals.reason: Richards' Gibson Les Paul Custom and Firebird VII are both well documented for this era but not pinned to this exact RCA Hollywood session by a primary source; likewise, the Vox AC30's presence at this specific US session (versus a local/rented amp) is plausible but unconfirmed.
proposals.whenToUse: Before treating the guitar model or amp choice as certain rather than era-plausible.
proposals.expectedGain: Higher-confidence sheet with fewer inferred details.
